title: Debugging Artifacts, Caches, and Releases
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of debugging artifacts, caches, and releases and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to debugging artifacts, caches, and releases.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on debugging artifacts, caches, and releases. For missing artifacts, stale caches, or release errors, compare configured names/paths and workflow run IDs, inspect retention and credentials, and verify published assets. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: For missing artifacts, stale caches, or release errors, compare configured names/paths and workflow run IDs, inspect retention and credentials, and verify published assets. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Missing upload files
items.text: For missing upload files, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Incorrect artifact names
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Failed artifact downloads
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

items.title: Cache key mismatches
items.text: Cache rebuildable dependencies using a key that includes the package manager, runtime/OS as appropriate, and lockfile hash. A cache miss must not change build correctness, and secrets do not belong in caches.

items.title: Unexpectedly stale outputs
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

items.title: Package publishing errors
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Release asset verification
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - name: Create report
    run: |
      mkdir -p output
      printf 'validation=passed\n' > output/report.txt
  - name: Upload report
    uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
    with:
      name: validation-report
      path: output/report.txt
      retention-days: 7
content_blocks.expected_output: The run produces a `validation-report` artifact containing `output/report.txt` with a seven-day retention period.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use this in a workflow that can run on a test branch. Never include credentials, environment dumps, or sensitive test data in the report.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and remove temporary workflow changes. If you triggered a real run, inspect the run log before editing the file again.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to debugging artifacts, caches, and releases. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain debugging artifacts, caches, and releases, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Turn run status, logs, and diagnostic data into a systematic troubleshooting process.

content.task: Apply debugging artifacts, caches, and releases to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: For missing artifacts, stale caches, or release errors, compare configured names/paths and workflow run IDs, inspect retention and credentials, and verify published assets. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: For missing artifacts, stale caches, or release errors, compare configured names/paths and workflow run IDs, inspect retention and credentials, and verify published assets.

Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
